title: Hubs and Spokes Along a Principal Cortical Gradient
excerpt: Semantic memory is organized along a macroscale principal connectivity gradient that runs from modality-specific sensory-motor cortices to transmodal integration hubs . At one extreme of this gradient lie the unimodal "spokes" - specialized cortical regions de
html:
Semantic memory is organized along a macroscale principal connectivity gradient that runs from modality-specific sensory-motor cortices to transmodal integration hubs 1. At one extreme of this gradient lie the unimodal "spokes" - specialized cortical regions devoted to processing a particular type of information (visual, auditory, motor, etc.). At the opposite end lie heteromodal "hub" regions (notably the anterior temporal lobes, angular gyrus, medial prefrontal cortex, and posterior cingulate/precuneus) which sit atop the cortical hierarchy and integrate inputs across modalities 1. This arrangement enables increasingly abstract, multimodal representations to emerge as one moves from the peripheral spokes toward the transmodal hub apex. In essence, the brain’s default mode network (DMN) - which includes these high-level regions - occupies the gradient’s transmodal end, whereas primary sensory and motor areas anchor the low-level end, with intermediate association areas in between 2. This gradient topography is thought to facilitate memory-guided and conceptual cognition, allowing heteromodal DMN regions to represent information in a format less tied to immediate sensory inputs and more grounded in stored knowledge 3, 2; however, the DMN should not be equated with the semantic network: while there is substantial anatomical and functional overlap (especially in ATL, AG, and mPFC), semantic cognition also relies on control regions outside the DMN, and DMN nodes participate in many other functions unrelated to semantics, including episodic memory, scene construction, and social cognition 3. The two systems dynamically couple or decouple depending on task demands, rather than forming a fixed one-to-one mapping. Structural connectivity matures along a sensorimotor-to-association axis (Figure) 38. Structural connectivity along the sensorimotor–association axis relates to cognition and psychopathology (Figure). A 2026 preprint maps cortical intrinsic timescales (Figure) 39.

Within the principal gradient, semantic knowledge can be understood via a "hub-and-spoke" architecture 4. Modality-specific "spokes" in visual, auditory, somatosensory, olfactory, and motor association cortices encode the raw features and instances of experience-for example, the sound of a waterfall in auditory cortex, its visual cascade of motion and color in occipito-temporal cortex, or the feel of its cool mist in somatosensory areas. These distributed representations converge via long-range connections onto bilateral, graded transmodal "hub" regions in the anterior temporal lobe (ATL), especially the ventrolateral and temporal pole zones, where unified, modality-invariant concepts of "waterfall" are synthesized 4. Crucially, when the ATL hub is damaged-most starkly in semantic dementia with bilateral ATL atrophy-the deficit is not merely naming: patients show a category-general, cross-modal degradation of conceptual knowledge, with impaired single-word comprehension, poor picture naming and word-picture matching, reduced knowledge of object features and use, and semantic errors for stimuli presented as words, pictures, and even environmental sounds; speech output and repetition are relatively spared early, yielding fluent but empty discourse 5, 6. Left-predominant ATL disease accentuates verbal semantic impairments (naming, single-word comprehension, exception-word "surface" dyslexia/dysgraphia reflecting over-regularization), whereas right-predominant disease disproportionately disrupts person-specific knowledge-recognizing familiar faces/voices and retrieving proper names and biographical facts-reflecting graded specializations across the bilateral hub 7, 8. The overall severity of the semantic deficit scales with the extent of bilateral ATL degeneration, and transient disruption of lateral ATL with TMS in healthy participants mimics the same amodal, category-general impairment profile 9, 10. White-matter tractography in semantic dementia further shows that multiple "module-to-hub" routes carrying written word, lexical, and face/object information into ATL are selectively compromised, and disconnection along these routes predicts semantic impairment severity 9, 11. A network study compares proposed and data-driven cortical memory networks (Figure) 40.

Another transmodal convergence zone is the angular gyrus (AG) at the temporo-parietal junction-part of the DMN’s heteromodal apex along the principal connectivity gradient, far from unimodal sensory-motor cortices 1. fMRI, lesion, and stimulation work converge on the view that AG encodes high-level, combinatorial situation meanings-event schemas and thematic relations that bind who-did-what-to-whom across modalities (e.g., the structure of "a wedding," "hammer hits nail," or "ordering coffee") 12, and it supports semantic integration/buffering that makes retrieval of well-learned associations feel effortless 13, 14. High-definition tDCS and patient work show a causal role for AG in integrating meanings during conceptual combination, while other recent studies link AG specifically to event-centric semantic structure rather than object-feature coding, which is stronger in ATL. In contrast, posterior MTG contributes more to controlled retrieval of weak links; disrupting AG selectively harms automatic retrieval of strong, highly related knowledge 14, 15. Consistent with this computational profile, the AG’s position at the transmodal end of the principal gradient (with ATL/mPFC/PCC) equips it to pool inputs from multiple ’spokes’ and stabilize abstract, generalized situation models during comprehension and memory.

Hub regions are densely connected to widespread cortical modules by major white-matter "highways," enabling the hub-and-spoke integration. For instance, the inferior longitudinal fasciculus (ILF) connects occipital visual areas to anterior temporal cortex, the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus (IFOF) links occipital and temporal regions to frontal cortex, and the uncinate fasciculus (UF) connects the ATL with orbitofrontal/vmPFC areas - all providing direct routes for modality-specific information to reach transmodal hubs. Likewise, dorsal pathways such as the arcuate fasciculus bridge temporal and inferior parietal regions with frontal cortex (supporting language and action-related semantics), and the cingulum bundle interconnects medial parietal, hippocampal, and frontal hubs along the DMN. Recent tract-tracing and neuroimaging studies have identified specific fiber pathways that implement this module-to-hub network: for example, direct tracts link the ATL to category-specific posterior areas (such as face-responsive fusiform cortex and word-form areas), effectively funneling visual and lexical information into the semantic hub 11. Damage to these hub-centered tracts in semantic dementia correlates with semantic impairment, whereas damage to more general ventral tracts (e.g. ILF or UF) has comparatively less impact. These findings reinforce a core principle of the hub-and-spoke model: semantic coherence is achieved by robust anatomical connections that allow distributed feature processors (the spokes) to converge on a central integrative network (the hubs). A tractography atlas maps the inferior longitudinal fasciculus (Figure) 41. The atlas also maps the uncinate fasciculus (Figure).

The semantic "hub-and-spoke" system is graded rather than monolithic: domain-biased spokes specialize by content yet stay tightly coupled to a shared, transmodal hub instead of operating as sealed modules. A left-lateralized fronto-temporo-parietal circuit (classically left inferior frontal gyrus, left posterior middle temporal gyrus, and intraparietal sulcus) comes online for tools and action semantics when you decide whether a wrench or pliers is better for loosening a bolt, simulate the grip sequence to use a corkscrew, or plan the hand trajectory to thread a wire through a tight space 16, 17, 18. Social and mentalizing semantics recruit a medial prefrontal-temporo-parietal network spanning mPFC, precuneus/posterior cingulate, and bilateral TPJ/pSTS when you infer a character’s hidden motive while reading a short story, detect sarcasm in a friend’s remark, or predict a teammate’s next move from gaze and body cues 19, 20. Scene and contextual knowledge are supported by a posterior-medial network centered on parahippocampal and retrosplenial cortex when you choose a route through an unfamiliar building, reorient using a distant landmark after taking a wrong turn, or recognize your street at night from its spatial layout and stable cues 21, 22. Together, these content-biased systems interface with the common hub to yield flexible, modality-invariant concepts that can be redeployed across tasks and contexts 23; in practice, they interact with transmodal integrators like the ATL and angular gyrus to enrich semantic representations with domain-specific detail. For instance, the PHC-RSC "place network" provides spatial context information that can be bound to more general event or object representations in the ATL or midline hubs. Similarly, the tool/action network in the left hemisphere contributes motor-pragmatic features of tool concepts, but it links into the ATL/temporal hub to integrate those features with an object’s visual and functional properties. The default mode network (DMN) - encompassing many of these heteromodal hub areas - plays a central role in orchestrating this integration. The DMN is often associated with internally driven cognition (e.g. episodic memory, imagination, narrative comprehension), and accumulating evidence indicates it is intimately involved in semantic processing 1. One proposal is that DMN regions collectively coordinate and synchronize activity across multiple modality-specific areas, effectively binding their features into a coherent, higher-order representation 3. In this view, the DMN acts as a global convergence zone that momentarily recruits local ensembles from visual, auditory, language, and other systems into a unified "neuronal ensemble" representing a situation or concept. The result of this large-scale synchrony is an integrated simulation of phenomenological experience - essentially, an embodied situation model that the brain constructs on the fly from diverse memory traces. For example, understanding a sentence or story involves the DMN weaving together word meanings, sensory contexts, and personal memories into a holistic mental scene. Such situation models are thought to be invaluable not only for semantic tasks like language comprehension but also for many cognitive functions not traditionally considered "semantic," such as imagining future events, navigating social interactions, or moral reasoning 3. By creating a richly textured simulacrum of experience, the DMN-driven hub network allows us to transcend the here-and-now, integrating what we know with what we perceive or imagine. This account finds support in neuroimaging studies showing DMN activation during semantic retrieval at sentence and discourse levels, and in the overlap between DMN regions and those engaged by autobiographical memory, theory-of-mind, and other high-level tasks (suggesting a common reliance on situation-modeling).

Within these integrated representations lie structured knowledge schemas - higher-order associative frameworks that capture abstract commonalities across our experiences 24, 25. In cognitive theory, schemas (a concept dating back to Bartlett 1932 and Piaget 1954) are mental models of the world that summarize typical patterns in a given context (for instance, the layout of a standard European city, the expected sequence of events at a neuroscience conference, or the characteristic behaviors of a sheriff in Wild West folklore). Schemas can be viewed as complex semantic memories: they organize concepts, relationships, and rules into a abstract templates that can guide our understanding and expectations in new situations; they represent information at a higher level of abstraction than single concepts - often encoding contextual and relational structure (who, what, where, when typically goes together) within a certain domain 26, 27 - and are highly flexible and generalizable. Once a schema is formed (e.g. a "restaurant schema" for the sequence of events in dining out), it can be applied to interpret or predict new instances (a meal at a brand-new restaurant) by filling in missing details with educated guesses 28, 29. This makes schemas powerful tools for directing attention to relevant details, facilitating memory encoding and retrieval (by providing an organized scaffold for new information), and even guiding problem-solving or exploration (by suggesting likely outcomes and strategies based on past patterns) 30, 25.

Neuroanatomically, schema processing centers on an mPFC/vmPFC-hippocampal axis that interfaces with posterior‐medial scene/context machinery (RSC/PHC) and parietal integrators (AG). mPFC/vmPFC expresses "schema templates" that bias encoding and retrieval toward prior structure and dynamically couple with the hippocampus; when vmPFC is damaged-especially in confabulators-patients fail to reinstate the correct script and over-accept schema-consistent lures (e.g., endorsing out-of-place "doctor’s office" details when judging a bedtime script), despite otherwise fluent behavior 25, 31, 32. Cross-species work shows that once a relevant schema is established, consolidation of new consistent information accelerates and shifts neocortical, vmPFC/ACC-dependent: rats with a learned flavor-place schema acquire new pairings in a single trial, and pharmacologically disrupting ACC/vmPFC plasticity abolishes this rapid assimilation-predicting that humans with medial prefrontal damage should show blunted schema benefits even when hippocampus is intact 33, 34, 35. The angular gyrus contributes the combinatorial "situation model" layer that stitches concepts into event schemas; perturbing AG causally slows or distorts conceptual combination (e.g., parsing "wet leaf," "wedding toast"), consistent with patients’ deficits on integrative semantic judgments when this node is compromised 12, 36. Finally, posterior‐medial cortex supplies the spatial-contextual scaffold that many schemas rely on: RSC/PHC lesions yield classic topographical/heading disorientation-patients become lost in familiar neighborhoods or can’t use landmark layout-reflecting a failure to instantiate the "place" component of situation models that would normally anchor scripts for wayfinding, scene construction, and narrative comprehension 22, 37.
